The most useful thing I tell people who are nervous about wine is that nobody at the table is testing you. I have poured wine for twenty years and I have never once heard a good conversation start with somebody listing grape varieties. What works is much smaller. Say whether you like it. Say what it reminds you of, even if it is something ridiculous. And then ask the other person a question, because the whole point of the glass is that it gives two strangers something to be curious about together. If you want one sentence that always works, it is this: have you ever had one from this region before? It is a real question, it is easy to answer, and it moves the conversation to the other person, which is where you want it. The people who look most comfortable at a wine dinner are almost never the experts. They are the ones who are genuinely interested and are not pretending to know more than they do.

I organize about forty corporate dinners a year, and the seating plan is the least of it. What I watch for is the first two minutes, because that is where the evening is decided. The thing that goes wrong is almost always the same. Somebody arrives, gets asked what they do, gives a job title, and then stops. Nothing else can happen after a job title. The people who are easy to talk to do something different: they give the title and then one small concrete thing beside it, something with a number or a place or a season in it, and the other person has somewhere to go. And here is the part nobody expects me to say. Guests who are not speaking their own language are usually the best company at these dinners, as long as they are willing to be a little slow. Slow is fine. Silent is what kills a table.
